title: ZTE denial order activated
summary: BIS activated a suspended denial order against ZTE after the company lied about disciplining employees involved in illegal shipments to Iran and North Korea. The order barred all US persons from exporting anything to ZTE for seven years, cutting off Qualcomm processors and Android licences and halting most of ZTE's production. ZTE settled in July 2018 for a $1 billion penalty plus $400 million held in escrow, a replaced board and a US-appointed compliance monitor. It was the first demonstration that a single US export order could shut down a large Chinese electronics firm within weeks.

title: Export Control Reform Act and FIRRMA enacted
summary: The Export Control Reform Act of 2018, enacted inside the FY2019 NDAA, gave the Export Administration Regulations permanent statutory authority and ordered an interagency process to identify and control "emerging and foundational technologies". The companion Foreign Investment Risk Review Modernization Act expanded CFIUS jurisdiction to non-controlling investments in critical technology. Together they are the legal foundation for every subsequent semiconductor control. BIS published its first emerging-technology advance notice three months later.

title: Fujian Jinhua added to the Entity List
summary: BIS added Fujian Jinhua Integrated Circuit, a state-backed DRAM start-up, to the Entity List with a presumption of denial, saying its new capacity threatened the viability of US suppliers of military DRAM. The listing cut Jinhua off from Applied Materials, Lam and KLA tools mid-installation and the project never reached volume production. It was the first use of the Entity List against a Chinese memory fab and the template for later chip listings.

title: Huawei and 68 affiliates added to the Entity List
summary: BIS listed Huawei Technologies and 68 non-US affiliates, requiring a licence with a presumption of denial for any export, re-export or transfer of US-origin items. The action cut Huawei off from Google Mobile Services, Intel and Xilinx parts, and from US EDA tools. BIS added a further 46 affiliates in August 2019 and 38 more in August 2020, taking the listed total past 150 entities. Huawei's handset business collapsed from about 240 million units in 2019 to roughly 35 million in 2021.

title: Foreign Direct Product Rule extended to Huawei chip designs
summary: BIS amended General Prohibition Three so that foreign-made chips are subject to the EAR when they are the direct product of US-origin software or technology and are designed by Huawei or HiSilicon. The rule reached TSMC's production of HiSilicon Kirin and Ascend parts even though no US content was in the chips themselves. TSMC stopped taking new HiSilicon orders within days and cut off shipments after 14 September 2020. This was the first time Washington used control of US design tools to block a foreign foundry from serving a foreign customer.

title: Huawei FDPR broadened to any chip made with US equipment
summary: BIS widened the May rule so that any foreign-produced item made with US-origin semiconductor equipment or software requires a licence when Huawei is a party to the transaction, whether or not Huawei designed it. It also added 38 more Huawei affiliates in 21 countries and let the Temporary General Licence expire. Because essentially every advanced fab uses Applied Materials, Lam or KLA tools, the rule made off-the-shelf merchant chips unavailable to Huawei too. It established the equipment-based direct product test later reused for the 2022 China-wide rules.

title: SMIC added to the Entity List
summary: BIS added Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation and dozens of affiliates to the Entity List, citing evidence of military end use. Licences for items uniquely capable of production at 10 nm and below carry a presumption of denial, while less advanced items are reviewed case by case. The listing froze SMIC's plan to buy an ASML EUV scanner, which had already been blocked at the Dutch licensing stage since 2019. SMIC nonetheless reached 7 nm using multi-patterned DUV immersion by 2022.

title: CHIPS and Science Act signed
summary: The CHIPS and Science Act authorised $52.7 billion for US semiconductors, including $39 billion in manufacturing incentives, $13.2 billion for R&D and workforce, and $500 million for international supply-chain work, plus a 25 percent advanced manufacturing investment tax credit. Recipients accepting incentives are barred for ten years from materially expanding advanced capacity in China or other countries of concern. Commerce ultimately signed awards worth roughly $33 billion, including about $6.6 billion to TSMC Arizona, $6.4 billion to Samsung Taylor and $7.86 billion to Intel.

title: First licence requirement on A100 and H100 exports to China
summary: Nvidia disclosed in an SEC filing that on 26 August 2022 the US government imposed a new licence requirement covering exports to China and Russia of its A100 and forthcoming H100 GPUs, and any product at or above A100 performance. Nvidia said up to $400 million of quarterly China revenue was at risk. AMD received a parallel restriction on the MI250. Nvidia responded within weeks with the cut-down A800, which kept the compute but dropped interconnect bandwidth from 600 to 400 GB/s.

title: October 7 rules on advanced computing and semiconductor equipment
summary: BIS created ECCN 3A090 and imposed China-wide controls on chips above 4,800 TOPS of aggregate processing performance combined with interconnect bandwidth of 600 GB/s or more, capturing the A100, H100 and comparable accelerators. Equipment controls covered logic below 16/14 nm FinFET, DRAM at 18 nm half-pitch or below, and NAND with 128 layers or more, with new foreign direct product rules extending them to non-US tools. US persons were barred from supporting the development or production of advanced chips at fabs in China without a licence, which pulled American engineers out of Chinese fabs within days. The interim final rule was published on 13 October 2022.

title: Dutch government announces DUV lithography export controls
summary: Trade minister Liesje Schreinemacher told parliament the Netherlands would impose national licence requirements on the most advanced immersion DUV lithography systems, following talks with the US and Japan. The letter named advanced immersion deposition and lithography as the target categories without naming ASML. ASML said the measures would cover its most advanced immersion tools, the TWINSCAN NXT:2000i and later, and would need Dutch government licences from 2023.

title: Micron barred from critical information infrastructure
summary: The Cyberspace Administration of China concluded that Micron's products failed a network security review and ordered operators of critical information infrastructure to stop buying them. Micron said roughly half of its China-headquartered customer revenue, about a low-to-high single-digit percentage of total company revenue, was at risk. It was Beijing's first direct retaliation against a US chipmaker and pushed Chinese buyers toward Samsung, SK hynix and the domestic supplier YMTC and CXMT.

title: Gallium and germanium export licensing
summary: MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2023 placed eight gallium-related and six germanium-related items under dual-use export licensing from 1 August 2023, on national security grounds. China produced roughly 98 percent of the world's primary gallium and about 60 percent of refined germanium at the time. Gallium goes into GaN power devices and RF parts; germanium into infrared optics, fibre and SiGe. Chinese gallium exports fell sharply in the following months and prices for both metals roughly doubled outside China.

title: Japanese controls on 23 categories of chipmaking equipment
summary: METI's amended export trade control order took effect, adding 23 categories of advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment to the licence list, covering cleaning, deposition, lithography, annealing and inspection tools. The controls apply worldwide but licences are effectively general for 42 friendly countries, so China is the practical target. Tokyo Electron, Screen, Advantest, Nikon and Canon were the main affected exporters. China filed a WTO consultation request over the measure in December 2023.

title: Dutch licence requirement takes effect for advanced immersion DUV
summary: The Netherlands' national technology export control list entered into force, requiring licences for advanced immersion lithography including ASML's TWINSCAN NXT:2000i and later systems, plus certain deposition and epitaxy tools. ASML said the measure affected a limited part of its China business and that it expected its 2023 shipments to be substantially unaffected. Chinese customers pulled forward orders through 2023, and China rose to about 46 percent of ASML system sales in the second quarter of 2024.

title: October 17, 2023 update closes the A800 and H800 workaround
summary: BIS replaced the interconnect-bandwidth test with a performance-density criterion, splitting ECCN 3A090 into a controlled tier .a and a notification tier .b, which captured the A800, H800, L40S and even the RTX 4090. Licence requirements were extended to companies headquartered in China or Macau wherever they are located, and to about 40 additional arms-embargoed countries, to stop transshipment. Equipment controls were tightened and the Chinese GPU designers Biren and Moore Threads were added to the Entity List. The rules were published on 25 October 2023 and took effect in stages from 17 November.

title: Graphite export licensing
summary: MOFCOM Announcement No. 39 of 2023 put high-purity, high-strength and high-density synthetic graphite and natural flake graphite products under dual-use export licences from 1 December 2023. China supplies about two-thirds of the world's natural graphite and over 90 percent of the anode-grade spherical graphite used in lithium-ion cells. Graphite is also used in crucibles, susceptors and hot zones for silicon and SiC crystal growth, so the measure touched the wafer supply chain as well as batteries.

title: Big Fund III capitalised at 344 billion yuan
summary: The third phase of the National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund was registered with 344 billion yuan, about $47.5 billion, the largest of the three phases and bigger than Phases I and II combined. The Ministry of Finance holds 17 percent, with China Development Bank Capital and the large state banks among 19 shareholders. Reporting indicated a heavy tilt toward equipment, materials and HBM rather than the fab-heavy allocations of earlier phases. Phase I raised 138.7 billion yuan in 2014 and Phase II 204 billion yuan in 2019.

title: Dutch controls extended to more DUV immersion tools
summary: The Netherlands expanded its national licensing regime to cover ASML's TWINSCAN NXT:1970i and NXT:1980i immersion scanners and related measurement and repair services, taking over from the US licence requirement that had applied to those models. The change took effect on 7 September 2024. ASML confirmed it did not expect a material change to its 2024 financial outlook because the tools were already restricted in practice. The move consolidated control of the mid-range immersion fleet under Dutch national authority.

title: Controls on GAAFET technology, quantum and advanced packaging tools
summary: BIS issued an interim final rule adding worldwide controls on quantum computing items, gate-all-around FET technology for advanced-node production, additive manufacturing for metal components, and certain electronic computer-aided design software. The rule created a licence exception for countries that adopt equivalent national controls, an explicit attempt to build a plurilateral regime outside Wassenaar. It complemented the Dutch and Japanese national lists issued in the same period.

title: December 2024 equipment and HBM package
summary: BIS controlled 24 additional types of semiconductor manufacturing equipment and three software tools, and for the first time controlled high bandwidth memory under ECCN 3A090.c, defined as memory with a bandwidth density above 2 GB/s per square millimetre, which captures HBM2E and everything above it. New foreign direct product rules extended the equipment and HBM controls to non-US production, with a de minimis approach reaching tools made anywhere. BIS simultaneously added 140 entities, mostly Chinese toolmakers, investors and Huawei-linked fabs including Naura, Piotech and SwaySure. The rules were published on 5 December 2024.

title: Outright ban on gallium, germanium and antimony exports to the US
summary: MOFCOM Announcement No. 46 of 2024, issued the day after the US equipment package, banned exports to the United States of gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials, and imposed stricter end-use review on graphite. Unlike the 2023 measures this was a country-specific prohibition rather than a licensing regime. USGS estimated the gallium and germanium ban alone could cost the US economy $3.4 billion in GDP. US germanium prices roughly doubled over the following year.

title: AI Diffusion Rule announced
summary: The Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion divided the world into three tiers: about 18 close allies with no caps, a middle group of roughly 120 countries capped at about 1,700 advanced GPUs per country without a licence and around 50,000 with one, and a denied group led by China and Russia. It created Universal and National Validated End User authorisations for trusted data-centre operators, and for the first time imposed controls on the model weights of closed frontier AI models. Published 15 January 2025 with a compliance date of 15 May 2025, it drew immediate objections from Nvidia and from allied governments.

title: Foundry due-diligence rule and Authorized IC Designer status
summary: BIS required foundries and packaging houses to apply a due-diligence test before making advanced logic dies for any customer, presuming a chip is destined for a restricted party unless the designer is an Approved IC Designer or the package is assembled by an approved OSAT. The rule followed the discovery that TSMC had produced an advanced die that ended up in a Huawei Ascend 910B. It set a deadline of 13 April 2026 to obtain Approved IC Designer status, later extended to 31 December 2026.

title: TSMC raises US investment to $165 billion
summary: TSMC announced at the White House an additional $100 billion of US investment on top of the $65 billion already committed in Arizona, for a total of $165 billion. The plan covers three more fabs, two advanced packaging facilities and an R&D centre, taking the Arizona campus to six fabs. TSMC said the expansion would support around 40,000 construction jobs over four years. The first Arizona fab had begun volume 4 nm production in the fourth quarter of 2024.

title: Export controls on seven medium and heavy rare earths
summary: Announcement No. 18 of 2025 put samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium, together with their oxides, alloys and permanent magnets, under dual-use export licensing, in direct response to the US tariff round announced two days earlier. China refines roughly 90 percent of the world's rare earth output and close to 100 percent of heavy rare earth separation. Licence processing initially took 45 working days or more, and magnet exports fell about 75 percent in May before recovering under a June trade truce.

title: H20 and MI308 put under indefinite licence requirement
summary: The US government told Nvidia that its H20, the China-compliant Hopper part built to the October 2023 thresholds, would require an export licence to China, Hong Kong and Macau for the indefinite future, on the concern that it could be used in supercomputers. Nvidia took a $4.5 billion charge in the April quarter and said it forgave about $2.5 billion of H20 revenue, with $8 billion of orders lost in the following quarter. AMD disclosed a charge of up to $800 million on its MI308. Nvidia had shipped an estimated $12 to $17 billion of H20s into China in the preceding year.

title: AI Diffusion Rule rescinded
summary: Two days before it was due to take effect, Commerce announced it would not enforce the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule and would replace it with a country-by-country negotiated approach. BIS issued parallel guidance that using Huawei Ascend 910B, 910C and 910D chips anywhere in the world risks violating the EAR because they were likely made with controlled US technology, language later softened from "anywhere in the world" after Chinese protests. Commerce also warned against allowing US AI chips to be used to train Chinese frontier models.

title: Gulf AI infrastructure deals announced
summary: During President Trump's Gulf trip, the US and UAE announced a 5 gigawatt AI campus in Abu Dhabi to be built by G42, with reporting that the UAE would be allowed to import the equivalent of about 500,000 Nvidia GPUs a year from 2025, roughly a fifth of them for G42 and the rest for US hyperscalers operating there. Saudi Arabia's new state AI company Humain signed agreements with Nvidia for several hundred thousand GPUs over five years and with AMD for a $10 billion programme. The deals replaced the rescinded Diffusion Rule's country caps with bilateral, security-conditioned arrangements.

title: H20 sales to China permitted again
summary: Nvidia said the US government had assured it that licences for H20 sales to China would be granted and that it hoped to begin deliveries soon; AMD received the same signal for the MI308. The reversal came after Jensen Huang lobbied the administration directly and argued that ceding China would hand the market to Huawei. Nvidia simultaneously announced an RTX Pro 6000D built for the Chinese market. Chinese regulators then discouraged domestic buyers from taking H20s on security grounds, and actual shipments stayed small.

title: 15 percent China revenue share for export licences
summary: Nvidia and AMD agreed to pay the US government 15 percent of their revenue from advanced chip sales to China in exchange for export licences, an arrangement without precedent in US export control practice. Analysts questioned its legality given the constitutional prohibition on export taxes. The deal covered the H20 and MI308. It set the template for the 25 percent arrangement later applied to H200 sales.

title: US takes a 9.9 percent equity stake in Intel
summary: The US government converted $8.9 billion of remaining CHIPS Act grants and Secure Enclave awards into 433.3 million Intel shares at $20.47, about 9.9 percent of the company, making Washington Intel's largest shareholder. The stake is passive with no board seat, and the government agreed to vote with the board on most matters. Combined with the $2.2 billion already disbursed, the deal accounted for $11.1 billion of Intel's federal awards. It followed SoftBank's $2 billion investment and preceded Nvidia's $5 billion stake in September 2025.

title: China finds Nvidia violated its antitrust law
summary: China's State Administration for Market Regulation concluded a preliminary finding that Nvidia breached the Anti-Monopoly Law and the conditions attached to its 2020 approval of the $6.9 billion Mellanox acquisition. Two days later regulators told ByteDance, Alibaba and other large buyers to stop testing and ordering Nvidia's China-market RTX Pro 6000D. Beijing paired the enforcement action with informal guidance that domestic AI firms should buy Huawei and Cambricon parts instead.

title: Affiliates rule extends the Entity List to subsidiaries
summary: BIS issued an interim final rule making any entity that is 50 percent or more owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more Entity List or Military End User parties subject to the same licence requirements. The rule closed a long-standing gap in which listed firms bought through unlisted subsidiaries, and it applied worldwide. Industry warned it could sweep in thousands of previously unlisted companies. Beijing called it a serious escalation, and Washington suspended the rule for a year on 10 November 2025 as part of the Trump-Xi trade truce.

title: Extraterritorial rare earth controls with a 0.1 percent rule
summary: MOFCOM issued Announcements 55 to 62 of 2025, adding holmium, erbium, thulium, europium and ytterbium to the controlled list, controlling rare earth mining, smelting, separation, magnet-making and recycling technology, and asserting jurisdiction over foreign-made goods containing 0.1 percent or more Chinese-origin controlled rare earths by value. Exports for military users face denial and exports for advanced semiconductor use, defined as logic at 14 nm and below or memory with 256 or more layers, face case-by-case review. The measures mirrored the US foreign direct product rule and were set to take effect on 1 December 2025.

title: Dutch government seizes control of Nexperia
summary: The Netherlands invoked the Cold War-era Goods Availability Act for the first time to suspend the authority of Nexperia's Chinese owner Wingtech, after the US affiliates rule brought the chipmaker within scope of the Entity List. An Amsterdam court suspended the Chinese chief executive and placed shares in trust. China retaliated on 4 October by blocking exports from Nexperia's Dongguan packaging plant, which finishes roughly 70 percent of Nexperia's output, triggering shortages of automotive discrete parts across Europe. The Dutch order was suspended on 19 November 2025 after talks with Beijing.

title: One-year truce suspends the affiliates rule and the rare earth regime
summary: Following the Trump-Xi meeting in Busan on 30 October 2025, BIS suspended the affiliates rule for one year until 9 November 2026 and China suspended the 9 October rare earth measures for the same period, along with the December 2024 ban on gallium, germanium and antimony exports to the US. China also agreed to issue general licences for rare earths, gallium, germanium, antimony and graphite for US end users. The US halved fentanyl-related tariffs on Chinese goods from 20 to 10 percent as part of the same package.

title: Section 232 proclamation puts a 25 percent tariff on advanced AI chips
summary: A presidential proclamation under Section 232 imposed a 25 percent tariff, effective 15 January 2026, on a narrow set of advanced computing semiconductors and products containing them that pass through the United States but are not destined for US use. The covered bands are chips with total processing performance of 14,000 to 17,500 and DRAM bandwidth of 4,500 to 5,000 GB/s, and 20,800 to 21,100 TPP with 5,800 to 6,200 GB/s, which capture the Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X. Eight use-based exemptions cover US data centres, R&D, start-ups, repairs, consumer and industrial uses and the public sector. The proclamation directed a review of data-centre chips by 1 July 2026 and signalled a second phase with higher rates and an investment offset.

title: H200-class chips move to case-by-case licensing for China
summary: BIS revised its licence review policy from a presumption of denial to case-by-case review for exports from the United States to China and Macau of advanced computing chips with total processing performance below 21,000 and total DRAM bandwidth below 6,500 GB/s, the band that covers the Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X. Approval is conditioned on certifications of sufficient US supply, third-party testing inside US customs territory, and know-your-customer and remote-access safeguards. Because the testing condition routes the chips through the United States, they also incur the 25 percent Section 232 tariff. President Trump had approved H200 sales in December 2025 while declining to allow the Blackwell-based B30A.

title: Chip licence requirement extended to Chinese firms' overseas units
summary: BIS issued guidance confirming that the licence requirement for advanced computing items applies to any entity headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau, or whose ultimate parent is headquartered there, even when the buying entity sits outside those jurisdictions. The clarification closed the route by which Chinese AI companies bought Nvidia and AMD systems through subsidiaries in Malaysia, Singapore and the UAE. Reporting put the volume that had moved this way in the hundreds of thousands of accelerators.

title: UAE moved to Country Group A:5
summary: BIS removed the United Arab Emirates from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and added it to A:5, granting Strategic Trade Authorization eligibility and a set of licence exceptions for chemical, biological and missile-technology controlled items. Licences are still required for advanced computing items under ECCNs 3A090.a and 4A090.a, except when consigned to UAE government agencies, to approved commercial entities listed in a new Supplement No. 8, or to US-headquartered AI companies and their UAE subsidiaries including Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI. The rule formalised the bilateral model that replaced the AI Diffusion Rule's country caps.
